note: Held areas and lines are approximate; during the civil war control was a patchwork of towns and villages, so blocks of Jewish settlement are drawn as areas, and ground that no force held is not shaded.

chapters.title: Partition and civil war
chapters.text: On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly voted to partition British-ruled Palestine into a Jewish state and an Arab state, with Jerusalem under international control. Jewish leaders accepted the plan; Palestinian Arab leaders and the Arab states rejected it, and fighting broke out at once between Jewish and Palestinian Arab militias. Through the winter Arab irregulars attacked Jewish convoys and besieged Jewish West Jerusalem, while both sides raided and bombed each other's towns and villages, but the map changed little.

chapters.title: April–May 1948: the Haganah offensive
arrows: Operation Nachshon opens the road to Jerusalem
Haganah takes Safed and eastern Galilee
Operation Ben-Ami: Acre and western Galilee
chapters.text: In April the Haganah, the main Jewish militia, went on the offensive under Plan Dalet. Operation Nachshon reopened the road to Jerusalem for a time, and Jewish forces took Tiberias, Haifa, Safed, Beisan and Jaffa, while the Gush Etzion bloc south of Jerusalem fell to the Arab Legion and local fighters on 13 May. Hundreds of thousands of Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled, many after the killings at Deir Yassin on 9 April. On 14 May, as the British left, Israel declared independence.

chapters.title: The Arab armies invade
arrows: Egyptian advance up the coast to Isdud
Egyptian column through Beersheba towards Jerusalem
Arab Legion takes position at Latrun
chapters.text: On 15 May the armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Iraq and Syria, with Lebanese and Saudi forces, entered the former mandate. Egyptian columns advanced up the coast to Isdud and through Beersheba towards Jerusalem; Transjordan's Arab Legion took the Old City of Jerusalem on 28 May and held Latrun on the road to the city; Iraqi troops held the hills of Samaria and Syria seized a bridgehead at Mishmar HaYarden. Israeli forces stopped the invaders and opened a bypass road to West Jerusalem before a UN truce began on 11 June.

chapters.title: The Ten Days
chapters.text: When the fighting resumed on 8 July, Israel attacked in the centre and the north. In Operation Danny it took Lydda and Ramle on 11–12 July, and most of their 50,000–70,000 Arab inhabitants and refugees were expelled or fled; in Operation Dekel it took Nazareth on 16 July. Israeli attacks on Latrun failed, and a second UN truce began on 18 July.

chapters.title: Operations Yoav and Hiram
arrows: Operation Yoav: breakthrough to the Negev
Operation Ha-Har south of the Jerusalem corridor
Operation Hiram in the upper Galilee
chapters.text: In mid-October Israel attacked in the south. Operation Yoav broke through the Egyptian lines, took Beersheba on 21 October and encircled an Egyptian brigade in the Faluja pocket, and Egypt then gave up Isdud and Majdal on the coast. In the north, Operation Hiram (29–31 October) drove the Arab Liberation Army out of the upper Galilee and occupied a strip of southern Lebanon; more Arab villagers fled or were expelled.

chapters.title: Operation Horev
arrows: Operation Horev: Auja and into Sinai
chapters.text: In late December Israeli forces attacked the remaining Egyptian positions in the Negev, took Auja on the border on 27 December and pushed into Sinai towards El Arish. Under British and American pressure they withdrew from Sinai, and the ceasefire of 7 January 1949 left Egypt holding only the coastal strip around Gaza and the besieged Faluja pocket.

chapters.title: The armistice lines of 1949
chapters.text: Israel signed armistice agreements with Egypt on 24 February, Lebanon on 23 March, Transjordan on 3 April and Syria on 20 July 1949. The lines, later called the Green Line, left Israel holding about 78 percent of former Mandatory Palestine, including the whole Negev, which its forces reached at Umm Rashrash (Eilat) on 10 March; Transjordan held the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and Egypt the Gaza Strip. Israelis remember the war as their War of Independence; for Palestinians it is the Nakba ("catastrophe"), in which about 750,000 people fled or were expelled and were not allowed to return.
